title: Quantisation of Angular Momentum — Bohr's Postulate and de Broglie's Proof
notes: The single postulate mvr = nh/2π — how Bohr used it, why it was 'ad hoc', and how de Broglie's standing waves turned it into a consequence (this bridge is also where the defects discussion begins).

Combined with the classical force condition $\frac{mv^{2}}{r}=\frac{kZe^{2}}{r^{2}}$, the quantisation rule fixes the allowed orbits: eliminating v gives $r_{n}=\frac{n^{2}h^{2}\varepsilon_{0}}{\pi m e^{2}Z}$ (numerically 0.529 n²/Z Å) and $v_{n}=\frac{2\pi ke^{2}Z}{nh}$. Without the rule, classical mechanics permits a continuum of orbits and no discrete spectrum.

The rule was *imposed*, not derived — no classical argument forces the angular momentum to come in packets of ħ. Critics (and Bohr himself) treated it as an arbitrary rule that happened to work. This is defect 'ad hoc postulates' in the limitations list.

If the electron is a wave of wavelength λ = h/mv, a stable orbit must be a **standing wave**: the circumference must contain a whole number of wavelengths, nλ = 2πr. Substituting λ gives n(h/mv) = 2πr → mvr = nh/2π — Bohr's condition *derived*, not assumed. For other orbits the wave interferes destructively with itself and the state is forbidden.

Even with de Broglie's justification, the orbit picture keeps a definite trajectory (definite r and p), which the uncertainty principle forbids — so the standing-wave argument is the *bridge* from Bohr to Schrödinger, not the destination: the wave must be treated in three dimensions, giving orbitals.

n = 1: mvr = h/2π = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Circumference 2πr₁ = 3.32 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and λ = h/mv = 3.32 × 10⁻¹⁰ m — exactly one wavelength fits the first orbit; n = 2 fits two, and so on. The integer n literally counts the waves around the orbit.
confusion: ❌ Bohr derived his quantisation from classical mechanics. ✅ He postulated it; de Broglie justified it in 1924.
❌ A non-integer number of waves still gives a stable orbit. ✅ Destructive interference destroys the wave; only nλ = 2πr orbits survive.
❌ Standing waves remove the uncertainty objection. ✅ They justify quantisation but keep the trajectory idea; Schrödinger's orbitals are needed for that.

universalFacts: One full matter wave fits the n = 1 orbit of hydrogen; n counts the waves.
de Broglie proposed matter waves in his 1924 thesis; the Davisson–Germer diffraction (1927) confirmed them.
Bohr's postulate predates de Broglie's derivation by 11 years — the clearest example of a successful ad hoc rule in physics.
examples: **Problem:** Compute the electron's de Broglie wavelength in the n = 1 orbit (v = 2.18 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹). **Solution:** λ = h/mv = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/(9.11×10⁻³¹ × 2.18×10⁶) = 3.33 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = 2πr₁ (r₁ = 0.529 Å) — the standing-wave condition verified.

summary: Bohr's second postulate, mvr = nh/2π, is the quantisation of angular momentum, and it is the hinge between the old and new models. Used with the classical force condition it fixes the allowed orbits — eliminating v gives rₙ = 0.529 n²/Z Å and vₙ = 2πke²Z/(nh) — whereas classical mechanics alone permits a continuum of orbits. The postulate was a defect because it was imposed, not derived. de Broglie (1924) removed that objection: if the electron is a wave of wavelength h/mv, a stable orbit must be a standing wave with a whole number of wavelengths round the circumference, nλ = 2πr, and substituting λ = h/mv returns mvr = nh/2π. For n = 1, λ = 3.32 × 10⁻¹⁰ m is exactly the circumference 2πr₁. Even so the picture keeps a definite trajectory, which the uncertainty principle forbids — so it is a bridge to Schrödinger's orbitals, not the destination.
importantConcepts: Quantisation of angular momentum: only orbits with mvr = nh/2π are permitted, n = 1, 2, 3, …
With the force condition it fixes the orbits: rₙ = n²h²ε₀/(πme²Z) = 0.529 n²/Z Å and vₙ = 2πke²Z/(nh)
Why it was a defect: the rule was imposed, not derived from any classical argument
de Broglie's rescue: the orbit must be a standing wave, nλ = 2πr, which derives mvr = nh/2π
Limitation that remains: a definite trajectory (sharp r and p) is forbidden by Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π
importantStatements: Classical mechanics alone allows a continuum of orbits; the quantisation rule is what makes the states discrete.
Only a whole number of wavelengths round the orbit is allowed — otherwise the wave interferes destructively with itself.
For n = 1 the de Broglie wavelength 3.32 × 10⁻¹⁰ m equals the circumference 2πr₁ = 3.32 × 10⁻¹⁰ m exactly.
The integer n literally counts the matter waves round the orbit.
Bohr's postulate (1913) predates de Broglie's justification (1924) by eleven years.

keyPoints: mvr = nh/2π with the force condition is the shortest route to rₙ and vₙ.
nλ = 2πr converts an imposed postulate into a derived consequence.
Non-integer wave numbers give destructive interference, so those orbits are forbidden.
Justifying quantisation is not the same as justifying the orbit — the trajectory is the next obstacle.
specialNotes: The standing-wave argument justifies only the quantisation of angular momentum, not the classical circular path.
de Broglie, not Bohr, supplied the justification; examiners check the attribution.
In three dimensions the wave is not confined to a circle, which is exactly why orbitals replace orbits.
